## Four climates in an hour: the farmer's journey

At half past six in the morning, when the light is still struggling against the sea mist, Manuel Gutiérrez starts his van in Motril with the thermometer reading fourteen degrees and a humidity that clings to the shirt. Fifty minutes later, after navigating a series of bends along the Gorgoracha road and crossing the gorge that heralds the Barranco de Poqueira, he parks in Capileira with three degrees on the asphalt and his breath turned to vapor. Gutiérrez, a farmer at the Valle de Lecrín cooperative, makes this journey three or four times a week during the harvest season, and describes it with the naturalness of someone who changes countries without changing regions: on the coast he picks avocados in short sleeves, and in the mountains he secures crates of snow for summer irrigation.

The geographical fact that underpins this routine is as simple as it is striking: between Motril and Capileira there are barely forty kilometers of road, but the cumulative elevation gain exceeds one thousand four hundred meters. This vertical distance compresses four climatic belts that at other latitudes would require an eight-hundred-kilometer journey north. The farmer who heads up at dawn passes through the thermomediterranean tier of citrus and subtropical crops, brushes against the mesomediterranean zone of olive and almond trees, ventures into the supramediterranean realm of chestnut trees, and, if the day demands it, reaches the oromediterranean level where vegetation disappears and only rock, ice, and silence remain. All this in less time than a Madrid office worker spends crossing the capital from end to end.

The accounts gathered at the Valle de Lecrín cooperative insist on a detail that disconcerts the visitor: the simultaneity of tasks. On the very same day in January, while one team packs Motril tomatoes into crates for the Granada market, another group ascends to the snowfields of Sierra Nevada to load blocks of compacted snow. That snow, protected with layers of straw and earth, will slowly melt throughout the spring and summer to feed the careo channels, an infiltration irrigation system introduced by the Berbers over eight centuries ago and which still functions without a single electric pump. The cooperative is no folkloric entity: it manages three hundred hectares spread across four municipalities and generates a turnover of over two million euros annually, but its logistics depend on an agricultural calendar that no agricultural engineer ever designed on paper.

That staggered calendar is the true wealth of the region. In January and February, the coastal greenhouses produce tomatoes, cucumbers, and green beans that ripen sheltered by the mild breezes of the Mediterranean. In May, when the heat starts to bear down in Motril, the cherry trees of Órgiva and Lanjarón enter full production at six hundred meters in altitude, where spring arrives a month later than on the coast. In October, the chestnut groves of Pampaneira and Bubión shed their burs at eleven hundred meters, just as the last watermelons are harvested in the Motril plain. A farmer with plots at three different elevations can string together harvests for ten months a year without leaving a twenty-five-kilometer radius.

The cooperative has embraced this as a silent competitive advantage. While the avocado growers in the Axarquía region of Málaga depend on a single crop and a single climate, the members of Valle de Lecrín spread the risk across the coast, the middle mountains, and the high mountains. If a late frost damages the cherry blossoms in Órgiva, the tomato harvest in Motril barely suffers. If a heatwave in August punishes the subtropical crops, the chestnuts in Pampaneira continue to plump up inside their burs unfazed. This diversification is not a recent strategy: the cooperative's records, founded in 1962, show that as early as the 1970s members were combining coastal sugarcane with mid-slope table grapes and late-season mountain potatoes.

The farmer's journey, however, is no scenic drive. The road linking Motril to Capileira passes through sections of tight bends where a lapse in concentration is dearly paid for, and in winter the snow forces the use of chains for the last few kilometers. The cooperative's vehicles are equipped with winter tires and folding shovels, and the drivers check the AEMET weather forecast with the same attention they give to market prices. Manuel Gutiérrez sums it up with a phrase that circulates among the members: you don't head up to the sierra for the fun of it, you head up because the sierra pays. The harshness of the journey is part of the price the region charges for its climatic diversity.

That harshness also has a physical dimension that the data do not gloss over. The elevation drop of one thousand four hundred meters in fifty minutes subjects both engine and body to abrupt changes in pressure and temperature that, repeated several times a week, take a toll on the joints and the ears. Older farmers speak of "sierra deafness," a passing discomfort that appears when descending too quickly from Capileira down to sea level. The cooperative has introduced mandatory fifteen-minute breaks in Órgiva for drivers making more than two trips a day, a measure not stipulated in any collective agreement but unanimously approved by the members in assembly.

The climatic contrast is also perceived in the clothing the workers carry in the cab. In Gutiérrez's van, a down jacket, a light raincoat, a cotton cap, and a pair of rubber boots coexist, each for a different stretch of the route. In Motril, the jacket is redundant; in Órgiva, the cap is appreciated; in Pampaneira, the raincoat may be necessary even if the sky is clear, because the gorge's humidity condenses on the slopes as evening falls; in Capileira, the down jacket is non-negotiable between November and April. That layered clothing is the textile translation of a territory that admits no simplifications.

The producers consulted insist that this staggered crop model is not exportable to just any mountain region. La Alpujarra brings together three conditions that rarely coincide: a subtropical coast less than ten kilometers from the peaks, a system of irrigation channels that distributes meltwater with millimeter precision, and a network of villages with enough population to sustain the workforce. Without any of those three pillars, the farmer's journey would be a picturesque anecdote rather than a productive system. With them, it becomes one of the clearest expressions of how geography commands and agriculture obeys.
